subject.title: The Return of the Muses
subject.author: Barbara Guest
subject.text:
So much goes away

              Forms are now shades,
              those solid weights, how empty they are,
              mere boxes,
              the whispering voice,
              the ankle bone only an arch.

              Peasants once sowed this valley
              there isn't any wheat here or oats
              there almost isn't a valley,
              only a dent.

              This morning was all concaveness,
              the clouds drew back into themselves,
              the clouds went so far away leaving it blue,
              now we're quite convex
              and the rain is emptying itself out on me

              The rain that took weeks to return,
              the rain that left us on Wednesday
              after tears, after dark, after that sluicing
              about in memory, fishing up

              The rain is here now.

              'It makes for change and a certain disagreeableness
              this coming and going makes one nervous'

. The farewells to buildings
              and then to the hole in the ground


 This hello on one's lips
 to a new perspective
 finished by the end of the week,
 completed a fresh horizon line

 The earth is old, no longer fragrant
 those planets are promising,

 Goodbye, hello.

 Yet you who had vanished
 you trailing your garments
 who went away in that last March stanza
 not liking the violins
 or standing around waiting
 your arms circling each other's waists
 or the salt in your mouth
 where the sea was whipping itself up in the corner
 and foam falling like ash

 You departed divine Muses .
 without warning

 And I went on a diet
 I stopped eating regularly,
 I changed my ways several times

"strict discipline, continuous devotion,
 receptiveness"

 were mine.

 Here you are back again. Welcome.

 Farewell, 'strict, continuous, receptive'-

There's that old shawl in the corner
looking like a wave

There's a ringing in my ears
as ifa poem were beating on stone

The room fills now with feathers,
the birds you have released, Muses,

I want to stop whatever I am doing
and listen to their marvelous hello.

title: Welcome Back, and Farewell
standfirst: Barbara Guest wrote a poem about the muses returning after a long absence — and spent much of her own career waiting for the same thing to happen to her reputation.

sections.heading: Welcome, and Goodbye
sections.body: Guest's poem announces its subject almost as a stage direction: "Here you are back again. Welcome." The muses — capital M, plural, classical — have been away, and now they aren't. In between there is a diet. Nothing here is played for straightforward irony, and nothing is entirely earnest either: in the same handful of lines that mourn abandonment by the goddesses of poetry — "You departed divine Muses. / without warning" — Guest is also worrying about food and an old shawl in the corner, "looking like a wave." The poem's method is to let a classical apparatus and an ordinary domestic register share a sentence without apologising for either.

sections.heading: The Woman Among the Nine Men
sections.body:
In 1952 a poem Guest had sent to *Partisan Review* caught the attention of Frank O'Hara, and she found herself, more or less by accident of address and acquaintance, inside what would later be called the New York School — O'Hara, John Ashbery, Kenneth Koch, James Schuyler, a circle that took its bearings as much from the Abstract Expressionist painters around them as from other poets. Guest had her own standing with those painters directly: from 1951 she worked as an editorial associate and art critic at *ARTnews*, and for a period she served as poetry editor of *Partisan Review* itself.

She was also, as her biographers and later scholars agree, one of the movement's very few women. Of the sixty-five contributors across the two anthologies that did the most to canonise postwar American poetry — Donald Allen's *The New American Poetry* (1960) and Donald Hall's rival anthology the same period — only five were women, and Guest was one of them.

sections.heading: Sporadic Recognition, Most of It Late
sections.body:
Recognition, when it came, took its time and rarely announced itself. The Academy of American Poets' own retrospective on Guest describes a writer who received "only sporadic recognition along the way, most of it late," even while she "remained at the vanguard of the genre throughout her career." Her second collection, *The Blue Stairs* — the book that holds "The Return of the Muses" — was published in 1968, after her debut *The Location of Things* (1960) and a further volume, *Poems* (1962). None of the three made her famous.

Guest kept writing for another four decades, growing more abstract rather than less, publishing steadily into her eighties. It was only in her final years — the Frost Medal for lifetime achievement in 1999, then a belated championing by younger experimental poets who read her as a forerunner of Language poetry — that anything like matching recognition arrived. She died in Berkeley, California, in February 2006, at eighty-five.

sections.heading: Painters' Muses
sections.body:
As a critic, Guest spent the 1950s writing about painters for whom subject and abstraction were the same argument her own poetry would go on having with itself. She once described her ambition as wanting "to invoke the unseen, to unmask it" — a critic's sentence as much as a poet's, and one that fits a poem about muses who are never physically described, only felt: as rain, as a ringing in the ears, as feathers filling a room nobody has seen a bird enter.

The scholar Rachel Blau DuPlessis has written of how women poets of Guest's generation found "female figures... positioned in an asymmetrical binary system through which they are habitually left behind" — and the muse tradition is the oldest version of that asymmetry, service without art ever credited to the one serving. "The Return of the Muses" does not solve that arrangement so much as trade places within it. Guest is not the (usually male) artist attended by a silent, female muse. She is the one left waiting, working through "strict discipline, continuous devotion, / receptiveness," for figures she addresses as equals — and then dismisses, in the very next line, with the same phrase turned into a farewell.

sections.heading: An Old Shawl, a Ringing
sections.body:
The poem's engine is a return of weather as much as of goddesses: rain that "took weeks to return," a sea that arrives as "salt in your mouth," a room that fills at the end with feathers from birds nobody has watched enter. Nothing rhymes, and the lines break for breath rather than metre — spatial rather than musical, letting white space do a stanza's work, much as Guest's contemporaries said her poetry more generally used the page the way a painter uses a canvas.

The closing image is the plainest in the poem, and the strongest for it: no metaphor, just a wish to stop whatever she is doing and listen to a "marvelous hello." For a poet whose career largely ran on delay — of publication, of critical attention, of the wider recognition that mostly arrived after her death — a poem that ends by asking its reader simply to stop and listen reads less like a small ars poetica and more like a diagnosis, written decades early, of everything that came before and after it.
